Time Quintet: Time Quintet is fantasy/science fiction series of five young adult novels written by Madeleine L'Engle.
 A Wind in the Door: Wind in the Door is young adult science fantasy novel by Madeleine L'Engle companion book to "A Wrinkle in Time", part of Time Quintet.
 Close the Last Door: Door (Japanese: 最後のドアを閉めろ! , Hepburn: Saigo no Door wo Shimero! ) yaoi manga series written by Yugi Yamada. adapted into OVA directed by Tama. licensed in North America by Digital Manga Publishing published first volume in 2006.
 Kaze Hikaru: Kaze Hikaru (Japanese: 風光る , lit. "Shining Wind") Japanese manga series written illustrated by Taeko Watanabe. Set in "bakumatsu" period series follows Tominaga Sei, young girl poses as boy Kamiya Seizaburo join Mibu-Roshi (Special Police; later known as Shinsengumi). befriends sensei, Okita Sōji, who discovers her secret.
 Kaze no Stigma: Stigma of the Wind or Kaze no Stigma (Japanese: 風の<ruby ><rb>聖痕</rb><rp> (</rp><rt >スティグマ</rt><rp>)</rp></ruby> , Hepburn: Kaze no Sutiguma , lit. "Stigma of the Wind") Japanese light novel series written by Takahiro Yamato illustrated by Hanamaru Nanto. After death of author on July 20, 2009, story remains incomplete at twelve chapters. 24-episode anime adaptation directed by Junichi Sakata animated by Gonzo aired from April–September 2007. dubbed in English by Animax Asia under title Stigma of the Wind and by Funimation as Kaze no Stigma.
Four Winds of Love: Four Winds is overall title for series of six novels written by Compton Mackenzie, "The East Wind of Love" (1937), South Wind of Love" (1938), West Wind of Love" (1940), "West to North" (1942), "The North Wind of Love, Book 1" (1944) and "The North Wind of Love, Book 2" (1945), together constitute major fictional chronicle of first forty years of twentieth century main protagonist of hexalogy is semi-autobiographical character of John Ogilvie.

Rotterdam The Hague Airport: Rotterdam (formerly "Rotterdam Airport", "Vliegveld Zestienhoven" in Dutch), (IATA: RTM, ICAO: EHRD) located 3 NM north northwest of Rotterdam, is Netherlands' third largest airport serves city of Rotterdam The Hague and surroundings. airport handled over 1.6 million passengers in 2016 features scheduled flights to European metropolitan and leisure destinations. used extensively by general aviation several flying clubs and schools at airport.
 A13 motorway (Netherlands): A13 motorway is motorway in Netherlands connecting cities The Hague and Rotterdam. Rotterdam The Hague Airport next to A13.
 Lahad Datu Airport: Lahad Datu Airport (IATA: LDU, ICAO: WBKD) is airport in southeastern of Malaysian state of Sabah. airport, approximately 1 km from downtown Lahad Datu serves town of Lahad Datu and neighbouring districts Kinabatangan, FELDA Sahabat and Kunak. airport can accommodate aircraft large as ATR72 terminal building can handle up to 100,000 passengers annually. In 2016, airport handled 140,077 passengers and 3,713 aircraft movements.
 Exeter Airport: Exeter Airport (IATA: EXT, ICAO: EGTE), formerly "Exeter International Airport", airport located at Clyst Honiton in District of East Devon close to city of Exeter within county of Devon, South West England. In 2007 airport handled over 1 million passengers for first time, passenger throughput declined. In 2016 handled 847,257 passengers, a 3.1% increase compared with 2015. Exeter has CAA Public Use Aerodrome Licence (Number P759) allows flights for public transport passengers or for flying instruction. airport offers scheduled and holiday charter flights within United Kingdom and Europe.
Sofia Airport: Sofia Airport (IATA: SOF, ICAO: LBSF) (Bulgarian: Летище София, "Letishte Sofiya" ) is main international airport of Bulgaria located 10 km east from centre of capital city Sofia. In 2015 airport surpassed 4 million passengers for first time handled total of 4,088,943 passengers, a 7.2% increase compared to 3,815,158 passengers in 2014. In 2016, number rose to almost 5 million passengers. airport serves as home base for BH Air, Bulgaria Air, Bulgarian Air Charter and base for Ryanair and Wizz Air. Vrazhdebna Air Base of Bulgarian Air Force is also located at airport.
 International air travel from United Kingdom: International air travel from United Kingdom refers to commercial carriage of passengers between UK and rest of world. In 2008, London Heathrow Airport busiest international airport on handled 67,054,745 passengers more than total population of United Kingdom. 20 busiest airports in UK handled close to 230 million passengers in 2008 (185 million were international passengers). geographical size of UK means many flights domestic in are actually international (i distance from Heathrow to Charles de Gaulle Airport roughly same as distance between John F. Kennedy International Airport and Washington Dulles International Airport). London airports, Heathrow, Gatwick Stansted alongside Manchester Airport rank amongst world's busiest airports by international passenger traffic. According to 2008 statistics best served nations by direct flights from UK were France, Italy, Spain, United States Germany with 50, 34, 33, 31 and 29 respectively. Spain was nation saw most passengers arrive from UK in 2008, with total of 34,557,729 (almost double the number flew to United States)

Deeyah Khan: Deeyah Khan (Urdu: , ] , born 7 August 1977 in Oslo, Norway), is a Norwegian film director and human rights defender of Punjabi/Pashtun descent.
 Damien Dematra: Damien Dematra is an Indonesian movie director, novelist, script writer, producer, international photographer, and painter. has written 101 novels in dual languages, English and Indonesian, 81 films and TV scenarios, produced 48 films in various genres; among them is internationally distributed "Obama Anak Menteng" ('Little Obama'), the award-winning movie "Si Anak Kampoeng" ('The Village Boy'), "L4 Lupus, "the record breaking movie "Dream Obama", "I'M STAR", "Let's Play, Ghost", "Dorce Vs. Hantu", and documentary film: "Gus Dur the Final Year", "Obama and Me"," Captain Jihad".
 Sandi Simcha DuBowski: Sandi Simcha DuBowski is an American director and producer, best known for his work on the intersection of LGBT people and their religion, DuBowski directed 2001 documentary "Trembling Before G-d" the producer of Parvez Sharma's documentary "A Jihad for Love" (formerly known as "In the Name of Allah") (2007).
 A Sinner in Mecca: A Sinner in Mecca is a 2015 documentary film from director Parvez Sharma ("A Jihad for Love"). film chronicles Sharma's Hajj pilgrimage to Mecca, Saudi Arabia as an openly gay Muslim. film premiered at the 2015 Hot Docs Canadian International Documentary Festival to great critical acclaim. film opened in theaters in the US on September 4, 2015 is a New York Times Critics' Pick.
 Steven Stalinsky: Steven Stalinsky is an expert on Middle East, terrorism and terrorist use of Internet, and encryption technologies, served as Executive Director of the Middle East Media Research Institute (MEMRI) since 1999. Stalinsky has briefed staff of the White House, State Department, Homeland Security, Justice Department, Office of Director of National Intelligence, Defense Department, Capitol Hill and other institutions.Since 2006, his research has focused on detailing and developing strategies against cyber jihad, describing how terrorist groups such as Al-Qaeda, ISIS, and others use Internet, social media, and encryption for propaganda, recruiting, and hacking. He was early advocate of calling on tech community to take stronger action on removing terrorist content from their platforms and for creating industry standards to combat it.
 A Jihad for Love: A Jihad for Love (also known by working title In the Name of Allah) is a 2007 documentary film on the coexistence of Islam and homosexuality. film is directed by Parvez Sharma, produced by Sharma and "Trembling Before G-d" director Sandi DuBowski.
 Jihad: A Story of the Others: JIHAD: a story of the others is a 2015 documentary film by Emmy and Peabody Award winning Norwegian director Deeyah Khan. film is produced by Khan's production company Fuuse. "JIHAD" is the outcome of a two-year investigation by Deeyah and provides a view from inside about what it is like to be drawn into radicalism. documentary film sets out to provide insight into why some young Muslims in the West embrace violent extremism and go abroad to fight holy wars and in some cases why they came to reject it.

LECOM Park: LECOM Park is a baseball field in Bradenton, Florida spring training home of Pittsburgh Pirates named after 15-year naming rights deal signed with Lake Erie College of Osteopathic Medicine, main campus in Erie, Pennsylvania and also campus in Bradenton. Formerly known as McKechnie Field named for Bradenton resident and baseball great Bill McKechnie, led Pirates in 1925 and Cincinnati Reds in 1940 to World Series titles. was coach of Cleveland Indians in 1948. notable members of Baseball Hall of Fame Roberto Clemente, Willie Stargell, Bill Mazeroski, Babe Ruth Ted Williams Mike Schmidt, played at LECOM Park. stadium hosts minor league baseball games for Bradenton Marauders, Pirates' High-A club in Florida State League.
 Athletics Stadium: Athletics Stadium is a former minor league baseball stadium in Tulsa, Oklahoma. stadium known as Drillers Stadium until early 2014 adopted current name. From 1981 to 2009, Drillers Stadium was home to Tulsa Drillers, of Double-A Texas League. For Drillers Stadium hosted regular season baseball games between Oklahoma State University and University of Oklahoma in Bedlam Series.
 Dr Pepper Ballpark: Dr Pepper Ballpark (formerly Dr Pepper/Seven Up Ballpark) is home ballpark of Frisco RoughRiders Class AA minor league baseball club. Located in Frisco, Texas United States stadium has capacity of 10,316. ballpark is host to numerous functions minor league baseball games, including corporate and charity events, wedding receptions, city of Frisco events, church services. Local soft drink manufacturer Dr Pepper Snapple Group holds naming rights and exclusive non-alcoholic beverage rights in park.
 Newark Bears (International League): Newark Bears were a Minor League Baseball team in International League, beginning in 1917 at Double-A level.played in International League through 1949 season, except for 1920 and part of 1925 season. Bears' last four seasons in International League (1946–1949), were a Triple-A team, highest classification in minor league baseball played home games at Ruppert Stadium in now known as Ironbound section of Newark; stadium demolished in 1967 1932, 1937, 1938, and 1941 Bears recognized as among 100 greatest minor league teams of all time.
 Josh Holliday: Josh Holliday (born September 14, 1976) is American college baseball coach and former professional player in Minor League Baseball. Currently head coach of Oklahoma State Cowboys baseball team, hired to this position prior to 2013 season. In 2014, Holliday was Big 12 Conference Baseball Coach of the Year as OSU claimed conference regular season championship. Hollidays' Cowboys pulled OSU Cowboy baseball tradition out of fire faced Oklahoma on final weekend of 2017. team in danger of missing out of postseason for 1st time in Hollidays tenure at Oklahoma State. Cowboys swept instate rival Oklahoma Sooners (#2 seed going into region play) to claim last and final spot as 8th seed in BigXII Championship. Cowboys went back to traditionion won 2nd Big 12 tournament in schools rich baseball history. Cowboys won 16 straight Big 8 tournaments before formation of Big12. Cowboys became 1st eight seed (last seed) to win conference championship Holliday got his team in NCAA postseason for 5th time in his 5 years at school season was full of injuries from top to bottom Holliday and associated Head Coach and current (2016) assistant coach of the year Rob Walton put together pitching staff of magical. Cowboys luck run out sent to Arkansas Regional and went 0-2 losing game one to Regional champions Missouri State Bears on two out bottom of 9th walk off HR.Garrett Benge hit for cycle for Hollidays Cowboys wasn't enough. Garrett McCain named 1st team all-American 25th in Cowboys history one of five current Cowboys drafted in 2017 preceded by 11 from 2016 College World Series club. Giving Holliday 16 in 2 years. Cowboys went on end of year run seen lose six games in a row face 1st Oklahoma State team to finish under .500 in 40 years.The Cowboys finished 30-27 on year. 6-5 victory of Texas Longhorns Hollidays' 200th victory as head man of Oklahoma State.

Gainesville, Florida: Gainesville is county seat and largest city in Alachua County, Florida, United States, and principal city of the Gainesville, Florida Metropolitan Statistical Area (MSA). population of Gainesville in 2013 US Census estimates was 127,488, a 2.4% growth from 2010. Gainesville is the largest city in region of North Central Florida. also a component of the Gainesville-Lake City Combined Statistical Area, had a 2013 population of 337,925.
 Cooperative Living Organization: Cooperative Living Organization (formerly Collegiate Living Organization) or CLO in Gainesville, Florida, is one of oldest continuously operating independent student-governed cooperative living organizations in United States. 80-year-old organization has provided over 2000 financially disadvantaged students opportunity for University of Florida education while providing experience in independent and socially responsible living by pooled resources and self-governance.
 Florida's 16th congressional district: Florida's 16th congressional district is an electoral district for the U.S. Congress was reassigned in 2012, effective January 2013, to western Manatee County, Florida and Sarasota County. district stretches from Bradenton, County Seat, in Manatee County to North Port, in Sarasota County, the county's youngest and most populous incorporated city. city of Sarasota is the County Seat of Sarasota County.
 Mason, Michigan: Mason is a city in U.S. state of Michigan. named after state's first governor, Stevens T. Mason. As of 2010 census, city population was 8,252. It is county seat of Ingham County. Mason is the only city in U.S. that serves as a county seat ahead of a state capital, with the capital of Lansing also in Ingham County. Despite Mason being county seat, many county offices and courtrooms are located in Lansing.
 Tampa–Hillsborough County Public Library System: The Tampa–Hillsborough County Public Library System (THPL) is a public library system based in Hillsborough County, Florida.State Library of Florida is main library source for Government of Florida governs a large portion of Florida's public and private libraries. THPL is part of two larger library networks, Hillsborough County Public Library Cooperative and Tampa Bay Library Consortium, also includes Temple Terrace Public Library in Temple Terrace, Florida, and Bruton Memorial Library in Plant City, Florida. are 25 branches of the Tampa–Hillsborough County Library System, not including digital-only and mobile-only services. Services provided by THPL include (but in no limited to) internet access, public meeting room spaces, interlibrary loans, a Bookmobile, a Cybermobile for Spanish speakers, technology classes, adult literacy programs, and downloadable eBooks. Drive-thru windows for returns and hold pick-ups are located at the Jimmie B. Keel and Jan Kaminis Platt Regional Libraries. Tampa–Hillsborough County Public Library System is also a part of Hillsborough County government.
 Cumberland Homesteads: Cumberland Homesteads is a community located in Cumberland County, Tennessee, United States. Established by the New Deal-era Division of Subsistence Homesteads in 1934, community was envisioned by federal planners as a model of cooperative living for the region's distressed farmers, coal miners, and factory workers. While cooperative experiment failed and federal government withdrew from the project in the 1940s, Homesteads community nevertheless survived. In 1988, several hundred of community's original houses and other buildings, characterized by native "crab orchard" sandstone used in their construction, were added to the National Register of Historic Places as a historic district.

Fortress Series: Fortress is series of fantasy novels by science fiction fantasy author C. J. Cherryh published by HarperCollins. set in medieval fantasy world with 15th-century feel feature magic, sorcery, medieval warfare, politics other elements common to high fantasy subgenre. first book series, "Fortress in Eye of Time", published in 1995 followed by "Fortress of Eagles" in 1998, "Fortress of Owls" in 1999 "Fortress of Dragons" in 2000 "Fortress of Ice" in 2006.
 Pen name: A pen name ("nom de plume", or "literary double") is a pseudonym (or, variant form of real name) adopted by author printed on title page or by-line of works in place of "real" name. pen name may be used to make author's name distinctive disguise gender distance author from previous works protect author from retribution for writings combine more than one author into single author or for reasons related to marketing or aesthetic presentation of work. author's name may be known only to publisher, or may be common knowledge.
 C. J. Cherryh: Carolyn Janice Cherry (born September 1, 1942), better known by pen name C. J. Cherryh, is American writer of speculative fiction. written more than 60 books since mid-1970s, including Hugo Award-winning novels "Downbelow Station" (1981) and "Cyteen" (1988), both set in Alliance-Union universe. known for "world building," depicting fictional realms with great realism supported by research in history, language, psychology, archeology. Her series of fantasy novels set in Alliance-Union universe, Morgaine Stories, sold in excess of 3 million copies.
Lionel Snell: Ramsey Dukes is current well-known pen name of Lionel Snell, contemporary English magician, publisher author on magic philosophy. has also pen names Lemuel Johnston. Angerford and Lea, Adamai Philotunus Per Anum Ad Astra. His regular satirical column "The Satanist's Diary" published in magazine "Aquarian Arrow" during 1980s early 1990s under pen name The Hon Hugo C StJ l'Estrange included other pen names contributors.
 Jane Thayer: Jane Thayer (the pen name of Catherine Woolley, August 11, 1904 – July 23, 2005) was American writer. known best for book "The Puppy Who Wanted A Boy", basis of 1980s Saturday Morning cartoon series, "The Puppy's Further Adventures". Jane Thayer wrote 86 books for children many ("The Blueberry Pie Elf" "The Puppy Who Wanted a Boy for Christmas") become classics. prolific editor suggested publish works under pen name Catherine authored picture books under pen name Jane Thayer writing books for older children adults under real name.

Segugio Italiano: Segugio Italiano ] is an Italian breed of dog of the scenthound family. It comes in both short-haired and wire-haired varieties. It thought to be an ancient breed, descended in pre-Roman eras from progenitor scenthounds in ancient Egypt. In 2009 ENCI (the Italian Kennel Club) registered 4,500 specimens of short-haired variety and 1,740 wire-haired specimens, making this one of top ten breeds in Italy.
 Sapsali: The Sapsali (삽살이) is a shaggy Korean breed of dog. word is followed in Korean by either "gae" (meaning "dog") or suffix "ee"/"i", but most commonly romanized as "Sapsaree". Traditionally, these dogs were believed to dispel ghosts and evil spirits.
 Shisa: Shisa (シーサー , Shīsā , Okinawan: "shiisaa") is a traditional Ryukyuan cultural artifact and decoration, often seen in similar pairs, resembling a cross between a lion and a dog, from Okinawan mythology. In magic typology, they sometimes also be classified as gargoyle beasts. Shisa are wards, believed to protect from some evils. People place pairs of shisa on rooftops or flanking the gates to houses, with left shisa has a closed mouth, right one an open mouth. open mouth wards off evil spirits, closed mouth keeps good spirits in.
 Ba-Jia-Jiang: Ba Jia Jiang (八家將) originated from the Chinese folk beliefs and myths, usually refers to eight members of the godly realm.general understanding of origin of Ba Jia Jiang is derived from the existence of eight generals who performed exorcism of evil spirits for the Wufu Emperor (五福大帝). These eight generals became revered as gods of the underworld, represented as bodyguards or attendants for temples of nether Gods such as Dongyue Emperor (東獄大帝), Yama (King of Hell, 閻羅王) and Cheng Huang (the City Gods, 城隍). Gradually Ba Jia Jiang evolved to appear also as bodyguards to Wang Ye (Royal Lord, 王爺) and Matsu (媽祖), and at many other temples. Later on, believers at temples dressed up as Ba Jia Jiang in to defend the Gods. These actions evolved into Taiwanese folk activities, part of Wu Array (Military Array, 武陣) in Din Tao (Taiwanese troupes, 陣頭). Ba Jia Jiang is responsible for capture of ghosts and evil spirits, bringing safety and good luck, and providing protection. They contain a strong religious nature, and Din Tao (Taiwanese troupes, 陣頭) often seem as mysterious, threatening and serious. Some Ba Jia Jiang members have relations with Taiwanese gangsters.
 Nightmarchers: In Hawaiian legend, Nightmarchers ("huaka'i pō" or "Spirit Ranks," " 'oi'o") are ghosts of ancient Hawaiian warriors. On nights of Kane, Ku, Lono, or on nights of Kanaloa they said to come forth from burial sites to march out to past battles or to other sacred places. They march at sunset and just before sun rises. Anyone living near their path may hear chanting and marching, must go inside to avoid notice. They might appear during the day if coming to escort a dying relative to the spirit world.Anyone looking upon or seen by marchers will die unless a relative is within the marchers' ranks- some people maintain if you lie face down on the ground they will not see you. This is to show respect. However, if exiting area is fastest option, it is recommended. Placing leaves of the ti ("Cordyline" sp.) around one's home said to keep away all evil spirits, and will cause huaka'i pō to avoid the area. Another thing to always highly respect night marchers which can result in great things.

Gilbert du Motier, Marquis de Lafayette: Marie-Joseph Paul Yves Roch Gilbert du Motier, Marquis de Lafayette (] ; 6 September 1757 – 20 May 1834), in United States often known simply as Lafayette, was a French aristocrat and military officer fought in American Revolutionary War. close friend of George Washington, Alexander Hamilton, Thomas Jefferson, Lafayette key figure in French Revolution of 1789 and July Revolution of 1830.
 The Cellar (Enfield, North Carolina): The Cellar is historic home at Enfield, Halifax County, North Carolina. dates to early-19th century large two-story, five bay, frame dwelling with attached one-story kitchen exterior brick end chimneys steep gable roof. childhood home of Congressman and Confederate General Lawrence O'Bryan Branch (1820-1862). house visited by Marquis de Lafayette during grand tour.
 Bell-Sherrod House: Bell-Sherrod House is historic home at Enfield, Halifax County, North Carolina. built about 1859, two-story, rectangular, Italianate-style frame dwelling with Greek Revival-style front porch. shingled hip roof pierced by two interior chimneys sheathed in weatherboard. conservatory added about 1915. house restored about 1987.
 James H. Parker House: James H. Parker House is historic home at Enfield, Halifax County, North Carolina. built in 1882, two-story, three bay, Italianate-style frame dwelling side-gable roof with overhanging eaves features one-story porch with low-hipped roof supported by paired (tripled at corners) chamfered columns topped by built-up and scroll-sawn brackets. on property is contributing smokehouse (c. 1855, 1882).
Enfield, North Carolina: Enfield is a town in Halifax County, North Carolina founded in 1740. 2010 United States Census town’s population was 2,532 increase of almost 8% from population 2,347 at 2000 census oldest town in Halifax County once world’s largest raw peanut market. Enfield part of Roanoke Rapids, North Carolina Micropolitan Statistical Area.
 John Hamilton (American Revolution): John Hamilton (died December 12, 1816) was military officer in British Army commander of Royal North Carolina Regiment of Loyalist provincial volunteers during American Revolutionary War from 1777 to 1783. Prior to Revolution Hamilton successful merchant in Halifax, North Carolina with business interests throughout Province of North Carolina. Hamilton commanded soldiers in major engagements, including battles of Briar Creek, Camden, Guilford Courthouse, Yorktown. After conclusion of war Hamilton made British consul to Norfolk, Virginia, one of only three Loyalists to receive consular positions in newly created United States.

Colt McCoy: Daniel "Colt" McCoy (born September 5, 1986) is American football quarterback for Washington Redskins National Football League (NFL). drafted by Cleveland Browns in third round of 2010 NFL Draft after playing college football for University of Texas. member of San Francisco 49ers.
 Case McCoy: Casey Burl "Case" McCoy (born February 12, 1990) former American football quarterback for University of Texas Longhorns football team. started 16 games for Texas over three-year period amassing 9–7 record. known as younger brother of NFL quarterback Colt McCoy.
 Walter Camp Award: Walter Camp Player of the Year Award given annually to collegiate American football player of the year decided by National Collegiate Athletic Association Division I FBS head coaches and sports information directors under Walter Camp Football Foundation; award named for Walter Camp, important influential figure in development of sport. Three players won award twice: Colt McCoy of University of Texas in 2008 and 2009, Archie Griffin of Ohio State in 1974 and 1975, O. J. Simpson of USC in 1967 and 1968.
 David Neill: David Neill (born July 17, 1980) American college football quarterback for University of Nevada from 1998 to 2001. In 1998, set NCAA record for most touchdown passes in a season by freshman with 29 thrown record tied in 2006 by Colt McCoy Texas Longhorns broken following season by Sam Bradford of Oklahoma. Neill previously held school record for most completed passes with 763 since broken by Cody Fajardo (878). received attention from Jacksonville Jaguars and New York Jets of NFL opted for veterinary career left football prior to 2002 NFL Draft.
 Sports team: sports team is group of individuals play sports, usually team sports, on same team. Historically, sports teams people play sports been amateurs., by 20th century, some sports teams and associated leagues became extremely valuable with net worth in millions. Real Madrid rated by Forbes as world most valuable sports team at $3.26 billion USD. Some individual sports have modified rules allow to be played by teams.
 1983 Stanley Cup Finals: 1983 Stanley Cup Finals contested by Edmonton Oilers first-ever Finals appearance and defending champion New York Islanders fourth, and fourth consecutive, Finals appearance. Islanders win best-of-seven series four games to none, to win fourth-straight and fourth-overall Stanley Cup. fourth straight Finals of post-1967 expansion teams, first involving former World Hockey Association (WHA) team. most recent time defending Stanley Cup champion won cup four years in a row, first (and to only) time North American professional sports team won four consecutive titles in any league competition with more than twenty teams. Since 1983, no professional sports team on continent win four straight championships and no NHL team won more than two consecutive championships (most recently Pittsburgh Penguins in ).

The Mighty Handful: (Russian: Могучая кучка ), also known as The Five and The New Russian School, were five prominent 19th-century Russian composers worked together to create distinctly Russian classical music. Mily Balakirev (the leader), César Cui, Modest Mussorgsky Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov Alexander Borodin lived in Saint Petersburg collaborated from 1856 to 1870.
 Alexander Borodin: Alexander Porfiryevich Borodin (Russian: Алекса́ндр Порфи́рьевич Бороди́н ; ], 12 November 183327 February 1887) was a Russian Romantic composer of Georgian origin, doctor and chemist. one of prominent 19th century composers known as The Mighty Handful, group dedicated to producing uniquely Russian classical music, than imitating earlier Western European models.

Banksiamyces: Banksiamyces is a genus of fungi in the order Helotiales, with a tentative placement in the family Helotiaceae. The genus contains four species, which grow on the seed follicles of the dead infructescences or "cones" of various species of "Banksia", a genus in the plant family Proteaceae endemic to Australia. Fruit bodies of the fungus appear as small (typically less than 10 mm diameter), shallow dark cups on the follicles of the "Banksia" fruit. Specimens continued to be collected occasionally for almost 100 years before becoming examined more critically in the early 1980s, leading to the creation of a new genus to contain what was determined to be three distinct species, "B. katerinae", "B. macrocarpus", and "B. toomansis". A fourth species, "B. maccannii", was added in 1984.

Wild Mountain Thyme: "Wild Mountain Thyme" (also known as "Purple Heather" and "Will Ye Go, Lassie, Go?")  is a Scottish folk song that was collected by Francis McPeake 1st, who wrote the song himself for his wife. The lyrics and melody are a variant of the song "The Braes of Balquhither" by Scottish poet Robert Tannahill (1774–1810), a contemporary of Robert Burns. Tannahill's original song, first published in Robert Archibald Smith's "Scottish Minstrel" (1821–24), is about the hills ("braes") around Balquhidder near Lochearnhead. Like Burns, Tannahill collected and adapted traditional songs, and "The Braes of Balquhither" may have been based on the traditional song "The Braes o' Bowhether".

 Armageddon in Retrospect: Armageddon in Retrospect is collection of short stories and essays about war and peace written by Kurt Vonnegut. first posthumous collection of his previously unpublished writings. book includes introduction by Mark Vonnegut, a letter from Kurt to his family about experiences as American prisoner of war in Nazi Germany, and fire-bombing of Dresden. It is a fretless instrument to produce the continuous slides between notes known as meend (glissandi), are important in Indian music.
 Apratim Majumdar: Apratim Majumdar (born 1978), is an Indian classical musician from Kolkata, India. He plays the Sarod. His "Dhrupadee Veenkar" style of Ustad Alauddin Khan's Seni Veenkar Gharana: analytically imaginative prosodic progression with metrical waves of melodic phrases interwoven with highest order of technical brilliance and maturity reminds the great legends of the Gharana. He is an internationally recognized instructor of classical Indian music.
 Sousaphone: The sousaphone ( ), is a brass instrument in the same family as the more widely known tuba. Like the tuba, sound is produced by moving air past the lips, causing them to vibrate or "buzz" into a large cupped mouthpiece. Because of the ease of carrying and the direction of sound, it is widely employed in marching bands, as various other musical genres.

Winnie the Pooh (song): musically emblematic of most successful branding Disney currently owns used in most merchandising models of brand since song's first publication in 1966 in musical film featurette "Winnie the Pooh and the Honey Tree". In film, song generally utilized in title sequence. song used in every theatrically released Pooh film most of television series. music video released for this version included in "The Many Adventures of Winnie the Pooh" DVD.
 The Wonderful Thing About Tiggers: Tigger's birthday believed to be in October 1928, year "The House at Pooh Corner" first published, on Tigger-related merchandise, Disney often indicates Tigger's birth year as 1968, a reference to first year Tigger appeared in a Disney production, "Winnie the Pooh and the Blustery Day". ", The Many Adventures of Winnie the Pooh ride and then again in 1977 release "The Many Adventures of Winnie the Pooh".
 Winnie the Pooh and the Blustery Day: featurette produced by Walt Disney Productions released by Buena Vista Distribution Company on December 20, 1968 as a double feature with "The Horse in the Gray Flannel Suit". later added as a segment to 1977 film "The Many Adventures of Winnie the Pooh".
 Up, Down and Touch the Ground: song also subsequently incorporated into 1977 musical film, "The Many Adventures of Winnie the Pooh" an amalgamation of three previous Winnie-the-Pooh featurettes including "The Honey Tree".

Berger Blanc Suisse: The Berger Blanc Suisse (English: White Swiss Shepherd , German: "Weisser Schweizer Schäferhund" , Italian: "Pastore Svizzero Bianco" ) is a breed of dog from Switzerland. It is of the same origins as the White Shepherd and the German Shepherd Dog, and has been recognized as a separate breed by the FCI.

Pandikona: The Pandikona is a primitive-type hunting dog from Pattikonda taluk-Kurnool district of Andhra Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh state, India. "Pandikona" is a medium size sight hound which is adapted to harsh climatic conditions of Kurnool district. This breed is associated with shepherd families of that region. PandiKona dogs need very little care.

Prosthetic Neuronal Memory Silicon Chips: Berger started to work on this chip in the early 1990s. While researchers are well into developing an actual memory prosthesis in animals, they still need to show that their chips can form long-term memories in many different behavioral situations. Berger hopes to eventually use these chips as electronic implants for humans whose brains that suffer from diseases such as Alzheimer's that disrupt neuronal networks.

Classical realism (international relations): Classical Realism is a theory of International Relations established in the post-World War II era that seeks to explain international politics as a result of human nature. The theory is associated with thinkers such as Niccolò Machiavelli and Thomas Hobbes. Modern thinkers associated with classical realism are Carl von Clausewitz, Hans Morgenthau and Reinhold Niebuhr. Classical Realist thought has since been overshadowed by Neorealism after Kenneth Waltz' work became more widely accepted due to the rise of Structuralism in North American International Relations scholarship which favored the latter's emphasis on rationality rather than human nature as cause for political conflict.

On War: Vom Kriege (] ) is a book on war and military strategy by Prussian general Carl von Clausewitz (1780–1831), written mostly after the Napoleonic wars, between 1816 and 1830, and published posthumously by his wife Marie von Brühl in 1832. His 10-volume collected works contain most of his larger historical and theoretical writings, though not his shorter articles and papers or his extensive correspondence with important political, military, intellectual and cultural leaders in the Prussian state.

Absolute war: The concept of absolute war was a theoretical construct developed by the Prussian military theorist General Carl von Clausewitz in his famous but unfinished philosophical exploration of war, "Vom Kriege" (in English, "On War", 1832).

Hawker Hurricane: Hawker Hurricane is a British single-seat fighter aircraft of 1930s–1940s designed and predominantly built by Hawker Aircraft Ltd for Royal Air Force (RAF). overshadowed by Supermarine Spitfire, aircraft became renowned during the Battle of Britain, accounting for 60 percent of RAF air victories in the battle, and served in all major theatres of the Second World War.
 No. 1455 Flight RAF: No. 1455 (Fighter) Flight was formed at RAF Tangmere, West Sussex on 7 July 1941, equipped with Turbinlite Douglas Boston and Douglas Havoc aircraft. On operations they co-operated with Hawker Hurricanes of 1 Squadron and 3 Squadron. flight replaced with 534 Squadron on 2 September 1942.
 Supermarine Seafire: In concept, it is relatively comparable to the Hawker Sea Hurricane, a navalised version of Spitfire's stablemate, the Hawker Hurricane.

The Real Thing (Norwegian band): The Real Thing (1992-1995) was a Soul Jazz Band from Oslo, Norway, founded in 1992 when Sigurd Køhn and Palle Wagnberg formed the forerunner, The B3 Blues Band with Vidar Busk and Hamlet Pedersen. They changed the name when Staffan William-Olsson and Fredrik Carl Stormer joined the band. Størmer was replaced by Torstein Ellingsen in 1995, and Ellingsen again by Børre Dalhaug in 1998. Due to the sudden death of the band's saxophonist Sigurd Køhn in December 2004 The Real Thing was hibernating until a reunion in 2010.

Torstein Ellingsen: Torstein Ellingsen (born 7 August 1966) is a Norwegian drummer and music producer, known from a series of album recordings.

Norwegians: Norwegians (Norwegian: "nordmenn" ) are a Germanic ethnic group native to Norway. They share a common culture and speak the Norwegian language. Norwegian people and their descendants are found in migrant communities worldwide, notably in the United States, Canada, Australia, Argentina, Chile, Uruguay, Brazil, Mexico, New Zealand, United Kingdom and South Africa.

Turkish people: Turkish people (Turkish: "Türk ulusu" ), or the Turks (Turkish: "Türkler" ), also known as Anatolian Turks (Turkish: "Anadolu Türkleri" ), are a Turkic ethnic group and nation living mainly in Turkey and speaking Turkish, the most widely spoken Turkic language. They are the largest ethnic group in Turkey, as well as by far the largest ethnic group among the speakers of Turkic languages.

Sasanian Empire: The Sasanian Empire ( or ), also known as the Sassanian, Sasanid, Sassanid or Neo-Persian Empire, known to its inhabitants as Ērānshahr in Middle Persian, was the last period of Persian Empire (Iran) before rise of Islam, named after House of Sasan who ruled from 224 to 651 AD. Sasanian Empire, succeeded the Parthian Empire, was recognised as one of leading world powers alongside neighbouring arch-rival Roman-Byzantine Empire, for a period of more than 400 years.
 Farrukhzad Khosrow V: Farrukhzad Khosrau V was briefly king of the Sasanian Empire from March 631 to April 631. was the son of Khosrau II.
 Samo: Samo founded the first recorded political union of Slavic tribes, known as Samo's Empire ("realm", "kingdom", or "tribal union"), stretching from Silesia to present-day Slovenia, ruling from 623 until his death in 658. In 631, Samo defended his realm against the Frankish Kingdom in the three-day Battle of Wogastisburg.

Stone Brewing Co.: Stone Brewing is a brewery headquartered in Escondido, California, USA. Founded in 1996 in San Marcos, California, it is the largest brewery in Southern California. Based on 2016 sales volume it is the ninth largest craft brewery in the United States.
 Beer Wars: Beer Wars is a 2009 documentary film about American beer industry. In, it covers the differences between large corporate breweries, namely Anheuser-Busch, Miller Brewing Company, and Coors Brewing Company opposed to smaller breweries like Dogfish Head Brewery, Moonshot 69, Yuengling, Stone Brewing Co., and other producers of craft beer. Also covered is how advertising and lobbyists are used to control the beer market, implying harm competition and consumer choice.
 Microbrewery: A microbrewery or craft brewery is brewery produces small amounts of beer (or sometimes root beer), typically smaller than large-scale corporate breweries, and is independently owned. Such breweries are generally characterized by emphasis on quality, flavour and brewing technique.
 List of breweries in California: Brewing companies range widely in the volume and variety of beer produced, ranging from small breweries to massive multinational conglomerates.

2016–17 Iona Gaels men's basketball team: 2016–17 Iona Gaels men's basketball team represented Iona College during 2016–17 NCAA Division I men's basketball season. Gaels, led by seventh year head coach Tim Cluess, played home games at Hynes Athletic Center in New Rochelle, New York as members of Metro Atlantic Athletic Conference (MAAC). finished the season 22–13, 12–8 in MAAC play to finish in a tie for third place. defeated Rider, Saint Peter's and Siena to be champions of MAAC Tournament. received MAAC's automatic bid to NCAA Tournament where lost in the First Round to Oregon.
 2010–11 Iona Gaels men's basketball team: 2010–11 Iona Gaels men's basketball team represented Iona College during 2010–11 NCAA Division I men's basketball season. Gaels, led by first year head coach Tim Cluess, played home games at Hynes Athletics Center and members of Metro Atlantic Athletic Conference.
 2011–12 Iona Gaels men's basketball team: Gaels, led by second year head coach Tim Cluess, played home games at Hynes Athletic Center and members of the Metro Atlantic Athletic Conference.
 2013–14 Iona Gaels men's basketball team: Gaels, led by fourth year head coach Tim Cluess, played their home games at the Hynes Athletic Center and were members of the Metro Atlantic Athletic Conference.

Russian Revolution: Russian Empire collapsed with the abdication of Emperor Nicholas II and old regime was replaced by a provisional government during first revolution of February 1917 (March in the Gregorian calendar; older Julian calendar was in use in Russia at the time).
 Russia–United Kingdom relations: Russia–United Kingdom relations (Russian: Российско-британские отношения ) is relationship between the Russian Federation and the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland and it's overseas territories. Spanning nearly five centuries, it has often switched from a state of alliance to rivalry or even war. Russians and British were allies against Napoleon, and enemies in the Crimean War of the 1850s, and rivals in the Great Game for control of central Asia in the late 19th century. were allies again in World Wars I and II, although relations were strained by the Russian Revolution of 1917. were at sword's point during Cold War (1947–91). Russian big businesses had strong connections with the City of London and British corporations during the late 1990s and 2000s.
 Nicholas II of Russia: 6 May] 1868 – 17 July 1918) was the last Emperor of Russia, ruling from 1 November 1894 until his forced abdication on 15 March 1917.

Castle Air Force Base: Castle Air Force Base (1941–1995) is a former United States Air Force Strategic Air Command base located northeast of Atwater, northwest of Merced and about 115 miles (185 km) south of Sacramento, California.

Sierra Academy of Aeronautics: The Sierra Academy of Aeronautics is an aviation flight school headquartered in Atwater, California. It operates its training facility at the former Castle Air Force Base in Atwater, California. Sierra Academy is also contracted by several foreign air carriers to perform pilot training, including Shanghai Airlines.

ATP Flight School: ATP Flight School, headquartered in Jacksonville, Florida, is the largest flight training company in the United States. The privately held company was founded in Atlanta, GA by its current management, a small group of airline pilots, in 1984. ATP’s initial focus was providing flight training to U.S. military pilots who were seeking their Airline Transport Pilot Certificates to transition over to commercial air carrier operations. Today, ATP is the leading supplier of professionally trained pilots to the nation's regional airlines.

Baraki Barak: Baraki Barak is a town and center of Baraki Barak District, Logar Province, Afghanistan. It was also the former capital of Logar Province. town is in a mountainous area in the valley of the Logar River. The main road Ghazni-Kabul passes about 20 km to the West of the town.
 Baraki Rajan: Baraki Rajan (Dari/Pashtun: برکی راجان) is a town within the Baraki Barak District of Logar Province, Afghanistan. Baraki Rajan lies approximately 3 km south of the town of Baraki Barak, the capital of the Baraki Barak District. Baraki Rajan is the location of the largest bazaar in the Baraki Barak District, with over 1,200 shops and businesses, with a 50+ bed hospital near town center, making Baraki Rajan an important center for commerce within District.
 Baraki Barak airstrike: The Baraki Barak airstrike was a coalition airstrike occurred on August 26, 2011 in Eastern Afghanistan. Six Afghan civilians from the same family were killed in the air strike in the Baraki Barak district of Logar province, Afghanistan. Four insurgents and three Afghan army members were also killed.
 Logar Province: Logar (Pashto: لوګر ; Dari: لوگَر ) is one of the 34 provinces of Afghanistan, located in the eastern section of the country. It is divided into seven districts and contains hundreds of villages. Puli Alam is the capital of the province.

Crescent Range: The Crescent Range, sometimes referred to as the Randolph Mountains, is located in the White Mountains of New Hampshire in the United States. The highest peak in the range is Black Crescent Mountain, with an elevation of 3264 ft .

Mount Crescent: Mount Crescent is a mountain located in the Crescent Range of the White Mountains in Randolph, New Hampshire. It is 3,251 ft (991 m) high, and its summit is the second highest mountain summit in Randolph, after Black Crescent Mountain (3,264 feet, 995 m). Both mountains are in Randolph's Ice Gulch Town Forest. On the 1896 topographic map, Mount Crescent is shown as "Randolph Mtn."  with an elevation of 3,280 ft, and Black Crescent is shown as "Mt. Crescent" with an elevation of 3,322 ft.

Black Crescent Mountain: Black Crescent Mountain is a mountain in the Crescent Range of the White Mountains, 4.4 mi north of Randolph and 4.7 mi southwest of Berlin in New Hampshire. The summit is on the eastern boundary of the White Mountain National Forest.

Santa Cruz (Santiago): Santa Cruz's population are the top 20 and the top 25 populated places of the island which is larger than the oldest city on the island Cidade Velha, it is also the fourth most populated place in the municipality as of 2010.

Stuart Roosa: Stuart Allen "Stu" Roosa (August 16, 1933 – December 12, 1994), (Col, USAF), was an American aeronautical engineer, United States Air Force pilot, test pilot, and NASA astronaut, was the Command Module Pilot for Apollo 14 mission.
 Moon tree: Moon trees are trees grown from 500 seeds taken into orbit around the Moon by Stuart Roosa during Apollo 14 mission in 1971. As Command Module Pilot on Apollo 14 mission, and was a former smoke jumper, Roosa was contacted by Ed Cliff, was the Chief of the Forest Service at the time, proposed the idea of taking seeds along.
 Apollo 16: second of-called "J missions," crewed by Commander John Young, Lunar Module Pilot Charles Duke and Command Module Pilot Ken Mattingly.
 Apollo 8: three-astronaut crew — Commander Frank Borman, Command Module Pilot James Lovell, and Lunar Module Pilot William Anders — became first humans to: travel beyond low Earth orbit; escape Earth's gravity; see Earth as a whole planet; enter the gravity well of another celestial body (Earth's moon); orbit another celestial body (Earth's moon); directly see the far side of the Moon with their own eyes; witness an Earthrise; escape the gravity of another celestial body (Earth's moon); and re-enter the gravitational well of Earth.

Nick Fury: Lisa Rinna plays Contessa Valentina "Val" Allegra de Fontaine, Sandra Hess plays Andrea von Strucker / Viper.
 Nick Fury (2017 comic book): Nick Fury is a 2017 ongoing comic book series published by Marvel Comics. series is written by James Dale Robinson primarily drawn by ACO. first series to feature Nick Fury Jr. as main character.
 Nick Fury, Agent of S.H.I.E.L.D. (feature): Nick Fury, Agent of S.H.I.E.L.D. was a feature on in the anthology comic "Strange Tales" introduced the fictional spy agency S.H.I.E.L.D. into the Marvel Comics world and reintroduced character of Nick Fury as older character from his currently running series "Sgt. Fury", was a WWII comic. feature replaced previously running Human Torch feature in book ran alongside the Dr.
 Fenris (comics): They are German twin children of supervillain Baron von Strucker of HYDRA and half-siblings of Werner von Strucker.

College Humor (film): College Humor is a 1933 American pre-Code musical comedy film directed by Wesley Ruggles starring Bing Crosby, Jack Oakie, Richard Arlen Mary Kornman Mary Carlisle. Based on story by Dean Fales film is about college professor and school's star football player become rivals for same beautiful coed. Released by Paramount Pictures film co-stars George Burns Gracie Allen.
 Bing Crosby: ( ; May 3, 1903 – October 14, 1977) was American singer and actor. Crosby's trademark warm bass-baritone voice made him best-selling recording artist of 20th century sold over one billion records, tapes compact discs digital downloads around world.

Fred C. Koch: Fred Chase Koch ( ; September 23, 1900 – November 17, 1967) was American chemical engineer and entrepreneur founded oil refinery firm later became Koch Industries, a privately held company under principal ownership and leadership of Koch's sons, Charles and David, listed by "Forbes," as of 2015, as second-largest privately held company in United States.
 Koch family foundations: Koch own majority of Koch Industries, oil, gas, paper, and chemical conglomerate US's second-largest privately held company.
 Dark Money (book): Dark Money: The Hidden History of the Billionaires Behind the Rise of the Radical Right (2016) is non-fiction book written by American investigative journalist Jane Mayer, about network of extremely wealthy conservative libertarians, foremost among them Charles and David Koch, together funded organizations to influence academic institutions, think tanks, courts, statehouses, Congress, American presidency for their own benefit.
 Koch family: Koch family ( ) is American family engaged in business, noted for political activities and control of Koch Industries, second-largest privately owned company in United States (with 2013 revenues of $115 billion).

New York State Route 9R: New York State Route 9R (NY 9R) is a north–south state highway in northeastern Albany County, New York, in the United States. Route 9 (US 9), connecting route to city of Cohoes 1.5 mi to the east. It leaves US 9 in hamlet of Latham and rejoins its parent in the hamlet of Boght Corners, both located in the town of Colonie. Most of NY 9R is a two-lane highway passes through residential areas;, the southwesternmost portion of route is four lanes wide and serves a commercial district. route was assigned c.
 Boght Corners, New York: Boght Corners (also referred to as Boght) is a hamlet in the town of Colonie in northern Albany County, New York straddles U.S.
 New York State Route 9N: Route 9 (US 9), NY 29, and NY 50 in the city of Saratoga Springs to a junction with US 9 and NY 22 in the Clinton County hamlet of Keeseville. It is concurrent with its parent route for 1 mi in the village of Lake George and for three blocks in the hamlet of Elizabethtown.
 Borodino, New York: Borodino is a hamlet located at the intersection of New York State Route 41 (East Lake Road, running approximately east-west) and New York State Route 174 (Rose Hill Road, running north-south) in the Town of Spafford in Onondaga County, New York, near Skaneateles Lake.

12 Years a Slave (score): 12 Years Slave is original soundtrack album to 2013 film "12 Years Slave" starring Chiwetel Ejiofor, Michael Fassbender Benedict Cumberbatch Paul Dano Lupita Nyong'o record contains twenty-one tracks from original film score written composed by Hans Zimmer. score admired contender for Academy Award for Original Music Score at 86th Academy Awards.
 Chiwetel Ejiofor: Chiwetel Umeadi Ejiofor, CBE ( born 10 July 1977) British actor. enrolling at National Youth Theatre in 1995 gaining scholarship to London Academy of Music and Dramatic Art at age 19 three months into course Ejiofor cast by Steven Spielberg play supporting role in film "Amistad" (1997) as James Covey.

Taj Mahal Bangladesh: Taj Mahal Bangladesh (Bengali: তাজ মহল বাংলাদেশ )is a scaled copy of original Taj Mahal (a Mughal mausoleum located in Agra, India) located 10 miles east of Bangladeshi capital, Dhaka in Sonargaon. Unlike the original, work on the building took only five years. The project cost about USD$56 Million, and was built 20 miles northeast of Capital Dhaka. Moni has explained he built a replica of the Taj Mahal so that poor of his nation can realise their dream of seeing neighbouring India's famed monument. This caused complaints from Indian officials, "You can't just go copy historical monuments" an official of Indian High Commission in Dhaka told press.
 Agra Fort: Agra Fort is a historical fort in the city of Agra in India. It was the main residence of the emperors of the Mughal Dynasty till 1638, when capital was shifted from Agra to Delhi.

Franco Corelli: Associated in with spinto and dramatic tenor roles of Italian repertory, he celebrated universally for his powerhouse voice, electrifying top notes, clear timbre, passionate singing and remarkable performances. Dubbed the "Prince of tenors", Corelli possessed handsome features and charismatic stage presence endeared him to audiences. He had a long fruitful partnership with Metropolitan Opera in New York City between 1961 and 1975. appeared on stages of most of major opera houses in Europe and with opera companies throughout North America.
 Tosca (1956 film): Tosca is a 1956 Italian musical film directed by Carmine Gallone starring Franca Duval, Afro Poli and Franco Corelli. based on opera "Tosca" by Giacomo Puccini. made at Cinecittà in Rome.
 La Bohème (1988 film): based on Giacomo Puccini's "La bohème".
 Jacopo Puccini: Jacopo (Giacomo) Puccini (] ; 26 January 1712 16 May 1781) was an 18th-century Italian composer lived and worked primarily in Lucca, Tuscany. was first of five generations of composers, most famous of was his great-great-grandson, opera composer Giacomo Puccini.

Project African Wilderness: Project African Wilderness (PAW) is a not for profit organisation with the express purpose of protecting and restoring the Mwabvi Wildlife Reserve in Malawi.
 Mwabvi Wildlife Reserve: With area of 135km2 Mwabvi Wildlife Reserve is Malawi’s smallest national park, and its least accessible., it has a wide variety of habitats, including Mopane, Combretum and brachystegia woodland, open savanna, dambo, and riverine areas. Mwabvi was the last natural home to Malawi's Black Rhino population, but both wildlife and woodland have been poached over recent years. many species of antelope, including kudu, sable, impala and nyala, are present, and even leopard and hyena have been seen. Buffalo still bathe in the Mwabvi river, and the number of human tourists is low, lions from neighbouring Mozambique are regular visitors. The scenery is spectacular, with views over the Shire River and Zambesi river, magnificent sandstone outcrops give an almost lunar feel to landscape.
 African buffalo: The African buffalo or Cape buffalo ("Syncerus caffer") is a large African bovine.

New Orleans Pelicans: The New Orleans Pelicans are an American professional basketball team based in New Orleans, Louisiana. The Pelicans compete in the National Basketball Association (NBA) as a member club of the league's Western Conference Southwest Division. The team plays their home games in the Smoothie King Center (formerly known as the New Orleans Arena).
 Jalen Jones: Jalen Jones (born May 27, 1993) is an American professional basketball player for the New Orleans Pelicans of the National Basketball Association (NBA). He was signed on a two-way contract with the NBA G League. He played college basketball for Southern Methodist and Texas A&M.
 Portland Trail Blazers: The Trail Blazers compete in the National Basketball Association (NBA) as a member club of the league's Western Conference Northwest Division. team played its home games in the Memorial Coliseum before moving to Moda Center in 1995 (called the Rose Garden until 2013). Trail Blazers have been the only NBA team based in the bi-national Pacific Northwest, after the Vancouver Grizzlies relocated to Memphis and became the Memphis Grizzlies in 2001, and the Seattle SuperSonics relocated to Oklahoma City and became the Oklahoma City Thunder in 2008.

Blues Traveler: Blues Traveler is an American rock band formed in Princeton, New Jersey in 1987. band's music covers variety of genres, including blues rock, psychedelic rock, folk rock, soul, and Southern rock. known for extensive use of segues in live performances, considered key part of re-emerging jam band scene of 1990s, spearheading H.O.R.D.E. touring music festival.
 Bridge (Blues Traveler album): Bridge is sixth album by American jam band Blues Traveler, released May 2001 (see 2001 in music). is Blues Traveler's first album following 1999 death of bassist Bobby Sheehan. album was originally titled "Bridge Out of Brooklyn."
 Blues Traveler (album): Blues Traveler, eponymous debut album from Blues Traveler, released on A&M Records in 1990. establishes band's trademark jam band sound featuring John Popper's harmonica.

Kinnaird Castle, Brechin: Kinnaird Castle is a 15th-century castle in Angus, Scotland. castle has been home to Carnegie family, the Earl of Southesk, for more than 600 years.
 Lady Charlotte Elliot: Lady Charlotte Elliot (22 July 1839 – 15 January 1880), born Charlotte Carnegie, was a Victorian poet born on 22 July 1839 in parish of Farnell, Angus (possibly at Kinnaird Castle), Scotland.
 Fra Lippo Lippi (poem): Fra Lippo Lippi is an 1855 dramatic monologue written by Victorian poet Robert Browning first appeared in his collection "Men and Women". poem, Browning depicts a 15th-century real-life painter, Filippo Lippi. poem asks question whether art should be true to life or an idealized image of life.

Battle of Berlin: The Battle of Berlin, designated the Berlin Strategic Offensive Operation by the Soviet Union, was final major offensive of European theatre of World War II.
 Alexander Nikolayev: Alexander Petrovich Nikolayev (Russian: Александр Петрович Николаев; 14 November 1918 – 13 June 2009) was a Red Army senior lieutenant and Hero of the Soviet Union. He received title Hero of the Soviet Union and the Order of Lenin for his actions during Battle of Berlin. Nikolayev also fought in Siege of Leningrad.
 Mikhail Linnik: Mikhail Nikiforovich Linnik (Russian: Михаил Никифорович Линник; 25 October 1916 – 21 December 2007) was a Soviet Army captain and Hero of the Soviet Union. Linnik was awarded title Hero of the Soviet Union and the Order of Lenin for actions during Lublin–Brest Offensive in September 1944.
 Georgy Vasilyevich Ivanov: Georgy Vasilyevich Ivanov (Russian: Георгий Васильевич Иванов; 25 May 1901 – 25 December 2001) was a Soviet Army major general and Hero of the Soviet Union. Ivanov was awarded title Hero of the Soviet Union and the Order of Lenin for leadership of 6th Guards Rifle Division from late 1944 to 1945. Ivanov fought in World War II at Battle of the Dnieper and Vistula–Oder Offensive.

Cale Gundy: Joseph Cale Gundy (born April 10, 1972) is a former American football quarterback who played for the Oklahoma Sooners from 1990 to 1993. While at Oklahoma he was a member of Delta Tau Delta International Fraternity. After coaching running backs for 16 years at Oklahoma Gundy was promoted to Assistant Head Coach and moved to Inside Receivers for the 2015 season. His brother, Mike, is the head football coach at Oklahoma State University.

Mike Gundy: Mike Gundy (born August 12, 1967) is an American football coach and former player. He is currently the head football coach at Oklahoma State University. Gundy played college football at Oklahoma State, where he played quarterback from 1986 to 1989. He became Oklahoma State's coach on January 3, 2005. In 2007, he received national media attention for his heated criticism of a newspaper article on one of his players.

Ike Mahoney: (October 25, 1901 – November 21, 1961) was an American football back who played five seasons with the Chicago Cardinals of the National Football League. He played college football at Creighton University and attended the Omaha High School of Commerce in Omaha, Nebraska. He was a member of the Chicago Cardinals team that were NFL champions in 1925. Mahoney played for the Chicago Bruins of the American Basketball League. He had received an offer to play baseball for the Pittsburgh Pirates but opted to play football for the Chicago Cardinals.

Nick Carter (musician): Nickolas Gene "Nick" Carter (born January 28, 1980) is an American singer, songwriter, actor, and dancer. best known as member of pop group Backstreet Boys. As of 2015, Carter released three solo albums, "Now or Never", "I'm Taking Off" and "All American" during breaks between Backstreet Boys schedules, and collaboration with Jordan Knight titled "Nick & Knight". made occasional television appearances and starred in own reality shows, "House of Carters" and "I (Heart) Nick Carter". gained fame in mid 1990s and early 2000s as teen idol. also older brother of singer Aaron Carter and late Leslie Carter.
 Brady Seals: Brady Seals (born March 29, 1969) is an American country music artist. Between then and 2002, recorded as a solo singer, releasing three studio albums charting in Top 40 on country charts with "Another You, Another Me".

Bayezid II Mosque (Amasya): Bayezid II Mosque (Amasya) is a historical 15th century Mosque in Amasya, Turkey. mosque was built in 1486 by order of Ottoman sultan Bayezid II, it is the largest Külliye of the city.
 Beyazıt Square: Beyazıt Square (Turkish: "Beyazıt Meydanı" ) is a square in the district of Fatih, situated in the European part of Istanbul, Turkey. It officially named "Freedom Square" ("Hürriyet Meydanı" ), but is known as Beyazıt Square after Bayezid II Mosque on one side of it. Square is the former site of Forum of Theodosius built by Constantine the Great. On one side of square is the main entrance of Istanbul University; Beyazıt Tower is on the university's campus and can be seen from the square. current form of square was designed by Turgut Cansever.
 Bayezid II Mosque: The Bayezid II Mosque (Turkish: "Beyazıt Camii, Bayezid Camii" ) is an Ottoman imperial mosque located in the Beyazıt Square area of Istanbul, Turkey, near the ruins of Forum of Theodosius of ancient Constantinople.

Greg Monroe: Gregory Keith Monroe Jr. (born June 4, 1990) is an American professional basketball player for the Milwaukee Bucks of the National Basketball Association (NBA). In his freshman season at Georgetown University, Monroe was named Big East Rookie of the Year. He was drafted by the Detroit Pistons in the 2010 NBA draft with the seventh overall pick and became the last Pistons player to wear the #10 jersey, after the Pistons retired the number for Dennis Rodman at halftime of a game against the Chicago Bulls on April 1, 2011.

Jerome Williams (basketball): Jerome Williams (born May 10, 1973) is an American retired professional basketball player who last played for the New York Knicks of the NBA. He was a star player on the Magruder High School basketball team. Drafted out of Georgetown University by the Detroit Pistons with the 26th pick of the 1996 NBA Draft (the pick originally belonged to the San Antonio Spurs and went to the Pistons in the Dennis Rodman trade), he played four-plus years with the Pistons, becoming one of their key reserves. He was a fan favorite during his days playing for the Toronto Raptors due to his tenacious efforts on the court.
